Instigate

IN-stih-gate / rhymes with navigate · verb

Hear It

What It Means

To instigate something is to be the one who starts or stirs it up, often trouble or conflict.

Investigators say a single email instigated the walkout.

Worked Example

After overhearing that the rival team had insulted their coach, one player instigated a full locker room confrontation by spreading the rumor before the coach could speak to calm everyone.

Instigate perfectly captures that this player is the originator—the one who deliberately starts the conflict. A word like trigger would just mean something caused a reaction, but instigate emphasizes being the trouble-STARTER who sets everything in motion.

How Instigate Sits Among Its Neighbors

Synonyms — open each to see how it differs

spark

spark: to set something off in an instant

stir

stir: to rouse feelings or trouble into motion

prompt

prompt: to cause someone to take an action

Antonyms

prevent

prevent: to stop something before it can start

defuse

defuse: to calm a situation before trouble erupts

How Strong Is It? — suggest → instigate → orchestrate → mastermind

suggest vs. instigate

suggest vs. instigate: Suggest is far weaker than instigate: suggesting merely floats an idea, while instigating actively stirs trouble into motion and gets it started.

orchestrate vs. instigate

orchestrate vs. instigate: Orchestrate is stronger than instigate — an instigator sets the trouble going, but an orchestrator carefully arranges every moving part of how it unfolds.

mastermind vs. instigate

mastermind vs. instigate: Mastermind is the strongest of all, beyond even instigate: the person who instigates lights the spark, while the mastermind designs the entire scheme from behind the scenes.

Build the Word

The pieces

Prefix — in-

Prefix — in-: in, on, toward (Latin)

Root — stig (from stigāre)

Root — stig (from stigāre): to prick, to goad (Latin)

Suffix — -ate

Suffix — -ate: verb-forming suffix: to make or do (Latin)

Put it together

Put it together: In- ('toward') plus stigāre ('to prick, to goad') plus the verb ending -ate: to instigate is literally to prick someone into action — the way a goad pricks an ox to make it move, an instigator prods trouble into motion.

Use the root in a new word: stick

Use the root in a new word: stick: The same ancient root meaning 'to prick or pierce' gives us the everyday word stick — a thorn sticks you the way an instigator pricks people into starting trouble.

Root Check

Word Choice

neutral / everyday

Use instigate when someone is the originator or deliberate starter of trouble or conflict. For milder stirring up of emotion, use stir or spark. For starting something neutral or positive, prompt or begin are clearer choices.
